prize_parts.citation: for a visionary prose of memory, body and dream, built on a poet's language and carried out on an architectonic scale in the Romanian novel

statement.case_for: I keep Cărtărescu first after reading my colleagues' openings, and the reasons are literary. His voice is recognisable within a few sentences. The Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy and Solenoid are built as large, deliberately patterned structures in which childhood memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation form one imaginative world. The sentence is the unit of that ambition, not plot or subject matter, and that makes the case a language case as well as one of scale. As I understand the public record, the poetry comes first and the prose grows out of it, so the oeuvre has a visible origin and an arc, not a single peak. He also stands in a European modernist line of the epic and the visionary. The prose is heavy and demanding, and I read that as the precondition of the work's reach and lightness, not a defect. This is the reading under which I rank him above the other candidates. On the common criteria of voice, formal and linguistic achievement, sustained quality, imaginative depth and significance across the whole body of work, he is the candidate whose case I can state most fully without leaning on reputation, politics or biography. Can Xue is a close second for me on originality of voice, and I weigh her case seriously.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is translation and corpus coverage. The case rests on dense, rhythm-dependent Romanian prose that I can judge only through translations of uneven quality and through public accounts of the poetry, which is less visible than the novels. There is also a real risk that the length and elaboration of the large novels shade into repetition or unevenness, which I cannot settle without reading the whole corpus. If the committee cannot be confident that the sentence-level achievement survives translation, the case would depend too much on architecture and imaginative scale, and those alone would not be enough.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first but warns that his long, intricate sentences make translated quality hard to judge and uneven between translators. She also asks whether the metaphysical density holds across the whole corpus or mainly in the best-known novels. She ranks Adonis second on formal and linguistic achievement, with the reservation that her assessment relies partly on reputation and secondary accounts.
responses.response: I agree with the translation caveat and apply it to my own case. It is why I treat the sentence-level claim as a judgment about the Romanian that I can only partly verify. The strongest evidence I can cite is structural: a trilogy and a later novel that are patterned across hundreds of pages, and a poetic origin that explains the prose texture. That supports a whole-career reading better than a single-novel reading, though I cannot call it proof. On Adonis I am more reserved than you, and I ranked him seventh. His influence on Arabic poetic language and tradition is clearly substantial. But the claim depends even more heavily than Cărtărescu's on prosody and intertextual play that translation largely loses, and his essays and cultural criticism are hard to separate from the poetry. You rely on secondary accounts, as I do. If you can say which specific poems or sequences carry the achievement in a way a non-Arabic reader can reasonably trust, I would reconsider my ranking.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Cărtărescu first for distinctive voice and sustained formal ambition. He ranks Can Xue last of his eight because he doubts whether her range of effects deepens across the work or repeats a single mode, and because only part of her large output is translated. He ranks Adonis second.
responses.response: I share your first-place judgment and take your reservation about Can Xue seriously, because I ranked her second and it is the main reason I do not rank her first. A deliberately uniform method is a real strength when it deepens and a real limit when it merely recurs. With so little of the Chinese output in translation, I cannot answer that for the whole body of work, and I would not claim to. Where I differ is on how much the doubt should count against her. Her uncompromising, dream-logic fiction is not like what other Chinese-language fiction does, and I think that distinctiveness deserves more weight than a last-place ranking gives it. I would keep her as the leading alternative and not discount her for translation limits that are the committee's own reading problem. Your high ranking of Adonis is useful, but in the form given it still leaves unanswered how a non-Arabic reader can assess the central claim.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first as the strongest case for a voice recognisable nowhere else. She also flags the risk that length and elaboration shade into repetition in some volumes. She ranks Pierre Michon third and Can Xue second, while ranking Marie NDiaye eighth.
responses.response: Your repetition worry is the right one, and I share it. What would reassure me is evidence that the later volumes extend the earlier ones, with new material and new formal solutions. The public summaries I have suggest a cumulative project, but I cannot confirm that volume by volume. On Michon we mostly agree, since I rank him fourth. The compression of his prose is a real achievement, but the very small corpus makes claims of breadth and development hard to sustain, so he stays below Cărtărescu for me. I place NDiaye third, well above your eighth. The case for her rests on the control of estrangement in the sentence and on two distinct strands, novels and plays. I admit that the scale and ambition are narrower, and I do not think she outweighs Cărtărescu, but I would like to hear whether you see the ambition as too limited or the translation access as too thin.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first for linguistic invention and sustained scale, and describes the major prose works as an integrated body, not isolated peaks. She ranks Lídia Jorge second and Louise Erdrich third, and she places Marie NDiaye seventh.
responses.response: I accept your description of an integrated body of work, and it is close to the criterion I care most about. I cannot, however, say that a coherent architecture proves the quality of each volume. As for Jorge, I did not rank her within my eight, so I cannot claim to have weighed her fully. I take your argument that her fragmented testimony and ironic narration give her a distinct voice beyond political subject matter. What I cannot judge is how singular that voice is among other Portuguese-language novelists, a doubt that Swärd also raises. I would need evidence of formal distinctiveness, not only historical seriousness, before I could move her up. On NDiaye, you rank her seventh while I rank her third. The difference seems to rest on how much weight the narrower scale should carry against the precision of her prose.

uncertainties: My assessment of Cărtărescu rests on public knowledge and translations. I have not independently verified the texts or read the Romanian originals, so the sentence-level claim is partly inferred.
Coverage of the poetry in translation is thinner than that of the novels, so the stated poetic base of the oeuvre is less certain than the prose achievement.
Whether the later novels extend the earlier ones, or the elaborate construction repeats itself, cannot be settled from public summaries.
For Can Xue and Adonis, translation covers only part of the corpus and cannot convey the original language, so my comparison with Cărtărescu is made under unequal evidence.
I have no way to judge how the citation scope would fit the will's reference to work of an idealistic tendency, and this is unresolved for every candidate on the list.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own literary and critical work on Central Europe is context only. It is not evidence for or against any candidate, and I have no recorded personal tie to any shortlisted writer.
